questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a wall painting on dry plaster must supply for itself.
questions.stem: In the brief for the assembly room, the wall is already dry when the painter arrives. What follows for the picture?

options.text: The paint must be held by a binder in the medium, since the dry wall will not absorb it.
The paint can be laid straight into the wall as if the plaster were still wet.
options.misconception: treats dry plaster as if it were still fresh

options.text: The painter must wait for the wall to be re-wetted before any colour is applied.
options.misconception: confuses painting on dry plaster with true fresco

options.text: The wall must be scraped back to the stone before the picture can be started.
options.misconception: invents a need to strip back to the masonry

questions.explanation: Paint applied to a dry wall has nothing to bind into, so the medium must carry its own binder and the film sits on the surface. Laying colour into dry plaster, rewetting it or stripping to the stone describe operations the brief does not call for.
questions.hint: Ask what will hold the paint to the surface.

questions.topic: Day-sized sections of a fresco wall
questions.learningObjective: Infer the working method from the joints between sections of a wall.

stimulus.body: The site record for the vestibule wall notes that the plaster was laid in horizontal bands of about 1.4 metres and that the painted figures stop sharply at the upper edge of each band.

questions.stem: Given the site record above, what does the sharp stop at each band indicate?

options.text: That each band was plastered and painted within a single working day.
That the painter stopped for a rest break each time a figure was completed.
options.misconception: explains the joints as working breaks

options.text: That the wall was painted in bands because the ladder was too short to reach further.
options.misconception: invents an equipment reason for the bands

options.text: That the upper part of each band was later wiped clean of its paint.
options.misconception: claims the paint was deliberately removed

questions.explanation: A hard edge where the painting stops and the plaster tone changes marks the limit of one day's plastering and painting. Rest breaks, ladder length and deliberate wiping would not produce a straight change of plaster tone.
questions.hint: Think about how long wet plaster stays workable.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A wall painting on a dry support
questions.learningObjective: Explain the advantages of painting a mural on canvas rather than on the wall.
questions.stem: In the brief, the mural is to be painted on canvas which is then fixed to the wall. Explain the advantages this method gives the architect.

answer.exemplar: Painting on a canvas that is later fixed to the wall lets the artist work anywhere in the studio, on a floor, on an easel or stretched flat, instead of on a ladder against a finished wall, and it removes the daily limit of how much fresh plaster can be laid. The finished cloth can also be replaced, and it can be rolled and moved if the room changes. The architect, in turn, gets a picture whose surface and joins are controlled rather than dictated by the building's own masonry.

questions.explanation: A canvas mural lets the artist work flat and at ground level, removes the daily limit of fresh plaster and can be replaced or moved. The architect gains a controlled surface instead of one dictated by the masonry.
questions.hint: Compare with painting on the wall itself.

questions.stem: The brief specifies a wall painting applied at 1.2 millimetres of wet paint over an area of 6 square metres. How many litres of wet paint does that passage require?

questions.learningObjective: Identify a one-point construction from measured convergence.
questions.stem: A survey of the foyer mural measures the orthogonals of the painted arcade. Every receding line meets at a single point 1.55 metres above the floor and 4.2 metres to the right of the doorway. What does this tell the architect?

options.text: The painting is built on a single vanishing point, so the space is constructed by one system.
The painter used two vanishing points, since the point of convergence lies outside the wall.
options.misconception: invents a second vanishing point

options.text: The arcade is drawn from a plan rather than from a viewpoint in the room.
options.misconception: claims the scheme comes from a plan

options.text: The mural is a direct copy of an arcade built on the far side of the town.
options.misconception: suggests the mural copies a real arcade

questions.explanation: Every orthogonal meeting at one point shows the arcade is built on a single vanishing point, the defining condition of one-point perspective. Two vanishing points, a plan-based scheme and a copied arcade would each contradict the convergence measured.
questions.hint: Count the points of convergence in the measurement.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Plan a tonal scheme that creates depth by atmosphere.
questions.stem: First, the architect asks that the far end of the painted hall be less distinct than the near end. Second, the painter must plan the palette. Which plan serves that aim?

options.text: Make the distant forms paler, cooler and softer in outline, and the near ones warmer and crisper.
Make the distant forms darker and heavier, so they read as solid mass at the back.
options.misconception: darkens the distance instead of lightening it

options.text: Paint the distant forms in the same tones as the near ones, since colour has no effect on depth.
options.misconception: denies that colour affects apparent depth

options.text: Outline the distant forms more sharply, so the eye reads them as further away.
options.misconception: reverses the treatment of the outlines

questions.explanation: Depth by atmosphere works by making distant forms paler, cooler and less sharply drawn than near ones, since the intervening air softens contrast. Darkening the distance, matching the tones or sharpening the outlines all work against the effect.
questions.hint: Think about what the intervening air does to contrast.

questions.learningObjective: Identify a dry-wall passage from the pattern of its losses.

questions.stem: Given the condition survey above, what does the flaked passage indicate?

options.text: That the passage was painted on dry plaster, where the film was never bound into the wall.
That the passage was painted on fresh plaster and has lifted away from it.
options.misconception: describes a dry-wall loss as a fresh-plaster loss

options.text: That the plaster beneath the flaked paint has been replaced with a filler.
options.misconception: invents a replacement plaster beneath the loss

options.misconception: blames the pigment colour for the flaking

A loss from fresh plaster, a replaced underlayer and an unstable pigment would not produce that pattern.
questions.hint: Ask whether the paint was bonded into the plaster or laid on it.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Day-sized sections of a fresco wall
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a large fresco wall cannot be painted in one week.
questions.stem: The brief asks the fresco painter to explain why a wall of 240 square metres cannot be painted in one week. Give the explanation.

answer.exemplar: Wet lime begins to carbonate from the moment it is spread, and the window during which it will accept pigment is a matter of hours, not weeks. A painter can therefore lay only a limited area of plaster and complete it before that plaster begins to set, which means a large wall must be divided into sections carried out on successive days. The joints between those sections are unavoidable, and the schedule of the whole wall follows the size of each day's work rather than the wishes of the architect.

questions.explanation: Wet lime carbonates within hours, so only a limited area can be plastered and painted before it sets, which forces the wall into sections worked on successive days. The size of the wall therefore dictates the schedule and leaves visible joints.
questions.hint: Think about how long wet lime remains workable.

questions.learningObjective: Judge which of two wall paintings was laid with a heavier body of paint.
questions.stem: Two wall paintings are compared. The first has a thin, transparent film that follows the trowel marks, and small areas of colour have been lost. The second has a surface that stands proud of the wall in ridges and holds the brush marks. Which was painted thicker?

options.text: The second, whose ridges and retained brush marks show a heavier body of paint.
The first, because a transparent film must necessarily be laid thickly.
options.misconception: equates transparency with thickness

options.text: Neither, since both were laid on the same plaster on the same day.
options.misconception: assumes both came from the same campaign

options.misconception: reads the trowel marks as evidence of thickness

questions.hint: Ask which surface stands away from the wall.

questions.learningObjective: Confirm a one-point construction from its converging orthogonals.
questions.stem: First, the architect's brief shows the orthogonals of the painted courtyard all meeting at one point on the horizon line. Second, the painter must confirm the device being used. Which statement confirms it?

options.text: The painting uses a single vanishing point, so all orthogonals are drawn to one point on the horizon.
The painting uses two vanishing points, so the orthogonals divide into two separate sets.
options.misconception: claims a second set of orthogonals

options.text: The painting uses parallel oblique lines, so the convergence is only a stylistic habit.
options.misconception: treats the convergence as decorative habit

options.misconception: dismisses the scheme as accidental

questions.hint: Count the points the orthogonals reach.

Outlining the distant forms with a hard dark contour so they stand out clearly.

options.misconception: relies on repetition rather than tonal change

questions.learningObjective: Interpret the height of a vanishing point relative to the painted room.

stimulus.body: The architect's note records that the vanishing point of the painted corridor is set 4 metres above the floor of the vestibule, while the floor of the painted scene itself is shown 1.6 metres above the vestibule floor.

That the vanishing point belongs to the real vestibule rather than the painted scene.
options.misconception: moves the point into the actual building

options.misconception: reads a raised point as a seated viewpoint

options.misconception: invents a second vanishing point from the height

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a dry-plaster passage flakes while a fresco beside it is sound.
questions.stem: The brief asks the conservator to explain why the passage painted on dry plaster is flaking while the fresco beside it is sound. Give the explanation.

answer.exemplar: On fresh plaster the pigment is carried into a wet lime that is in the act of hardening, so the colour becomes part of the wall and is locked in as the lime carbonates. On dry plaster there is no such chemical union: the paint sits as a film on the surface, held only by the binder in the medium and by whatever grip the wall offers. The result is a layer that can lift, flake and take the plaster with it, so the sound of the fresco is a matter of bond rather than of care.

questions.explanation: On fresh plaster the pigment becomes chemically part of the wall as the lime carbonates, whereas on dry plaster the paint is only a film held on the surface. The sound of the fresco is therefore a matter of bond rather than of the painter's care.
questions.hint: Compare what the lime does in each case.

The picture will outlast the wall, because a canvas cannot be affected by damp in the wall.
options.misconception: claims the canvas is immune to the wall's damp

options.text: The wall will carry more weight, since the canvas and its fixings add structure.
options.misconception: makes the mural a structural element

options.text: The scheme avoids all cracking, because a stretched canvas never moves with the building.
options.misconception: claims the canvas cannot move with the wall

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why paint on dry plaster must be laid thickly.
questions.stem: First, the brief specifies that the passage painted on dry plaster must carry a heavy body of colour. Second, the painter asks why that is necessary. Which explanation fits?

options.text: Because a thin film on dry plaster is easily lost, so the colour must be laid thickly to hold.
Because a thin film on dry plaster would sink into the surface like a true fresco passage.
options.misconception: treats dry plaster as an absorbent ground

options.text: Because thick paint on dry plaster becomes chemically bonded to the lime as it sets.
options.misconception: claims dry plaster carbonates with the paint

options.text: Because a thick film lets the painter remove errors later without damaging the wall.
options.misconception: claims thickness makes the work reversible

questions.explanation: Paint on dry plaster has no chemical bond and relies on the binder and on body for adhesion, so a thin film is easily lost and the colour must be laid thickly. Absorption, carbonation and reversibility are not what happens on a dry wall.
questions.hint: Ask what holds a thin film to dry plaster.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Identify atmospheric depth from a record of colour values and edges.

stimulus.body: The colour notes for the painted valley record that the far ridge is mixed from a light grey with a little blue, the middle fields from a mid green, and the near hedge from a dark warm green, and that the far ridge has no drawn contour.

questions.stem: From the colour notes above, which effect is being used to build depth in the valley?

options.text: Atmospheric depth, with the far forms paler, cooler and less sharply edged than the near ones.
Linear perspective, with the near hedge drawn larger to scale than the far ridge.
options.misconception: confuses the tonal scheme with a perspectival one

options.text: Chiaroscuro, with the near hedge lit from one side and the far ridge in shadow.
options.misconception: mistakes tonal change for modelled light

options.misconception: claims the values are held constant

questions.hint: Compare the values and the edges of the near and far bands.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how an off-centre vanishing point changes a painted space.
questions.stem: For the stair hall the brief places the vanishing point off centre, high on the wall. Explain how that placement changes the picture.

answer.exemplar: The vanishing point fixes the viewpoint, so placing it off centre means the scene is not seen from directly in front of the middle of the picture but from a point shifted to one side and raised. The recession then falls asymmetrically: the lines on the side towards the viewpoint converge more steeply while the lines on the far side run out more shallowly. The composition gains an oblique, less symmetrical address, and the viewer is placed in the room with the scene rather than in front of it.

questions.explanation: Because the vanishing point fixes the viewpoint, an off-centre and raised point means the scene is seen from an oblique and elevated position, so the recession runs unevenly to either side. The result is a less symmetrical, more engaged address to the viewer.
questions.hint: Think about what the position says about the viewer.

questions.learningObjective: Identify a one-point scheme from the behaviour of parallel and receding lines.

stimulus.body: The architect's note records that in the painted vestibule all the ceiling beams run parallel to the picture plane and do not converge, while the floor tiles recede to a single point.

It is a two-point scheme, since the ceiling beams run away from the viewer.
options.misconception: calls parallel beams a second set of orthogonals

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why one flat colour cannot serve near and far water.
questions.stem: The brief for the painted coastline asks why the painter must not use the same blue for the sea near the shore and the sea on the horizon. Give the explanation.

answer.exemplar: Atmospheric depth is built from a graduated change of colour, tone and clarity, and the painter has to plan that gradient in advance across the whole view. Using one flat blue for near and far water removes the graded shift that tells the eye how far away the horizon is, so the picture flattens into a pattern of shapes. Working the tones in planned steps also keeps the recession coherent when the picture is seen as a whole from the floor of the hall.

questions.explanation: Atmospheric depth depends on a planned gradient in colour, tone and clarity, and a single flat blue removes the graduated shift that makes the horizon read as distance. The picture then flattens into a pattern rather than a view.
questions.hint: Think about what a single flat colour does to the recession.

questions.learningObjective: Compare losses on dry and fresh plaster to identify what governs survival.

options.text: That the bond to the wall, not the paint itself, governs how well the passage survives.
That the pigments of the dry passage were of poorer quality than those of the fresco.
options.misconception: blames pigment quality for the difference

options.text: That the dry passage was painted by a less careful hand than the fresco passage.
options.misconception: attributes the loss to the painter's care

options.text: That the fresco passage was protected by varnish while the dry passage was not.
options.misconception: invents varnish on the fresco passage

questions.explanation: Two passages made with the same kinds of paint differ enormously in survival according to whether they were bonded into wet lime or laid on a dry surface, so the bond governs durability. Pigment quality, the painter's care and varnish each fail to explain the pattern.
questions.hint: Ask what the two passages have in common besides their paint.

About 4 square metres a day, because the days should be divided into the area.
options.misconception: divides the days into the wrong order

options.text: About 250 square metres a day, because the wall can be laid in one morning.

options.misconception: uses a smaller wall to reach the same rate

The picture becomes permanently part of the wall and shares its damp and movement.

options.misconception: links the smooth support to speed of work

options.misconception: invents a fire advantage for canvas

questions.learningObjective: Explain why a secco passage is heavier than the fresco passages beside it.

stimulus.body: The site record for the vestibule notes that the passage at eye level was left in a secco and has built up a thicker body of colour, while the surrounding fresco passages are thin and even.

questions.stem: From the site record above, why is the secco passage thicker than the fresco passages beside it?

options.text: Because paint on dry plaster has no bond and must be laid heavily to stay attached.
Because the fresco passages were polished down and the secco passage was left rough.
options.misconception: explains the difference by polishing

options.text: Because a secco passage is always painted twice to build up the colour.
options.misconception: invents a fixed number of coats

options.text: Because thick paint was specified for the parts of the wall people can touch.
options.misconception: invents a touch-based reason for the thickness

questions.explanation: Colour laid on dry plaster has nothing to bind into and depends on its own body for adhesion, so it is applied heavily, whereas fresco passages are thin because the wet lime holds them. Polishing, a fixed number of coats and touch are not the reasons.
questions.hint: Ask what holds each passage to the wall.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why orthogonals must reach a single vanishing point.
questions.stem: The brief asks the painter to explain why the orthogonals of the painted courtyard all meet at one point rather than being scattered. Give the explanation.

answer.exemplar: A single vanishing point is what gives a constructed interior its unity, because every line that recedes from the viewer is made to obey the same point and therefore to agree with a single, shared viewpoint. Scattering the convergence would produce a set of separate spaces that the eye cannot read as one room, since the lines of one wall would contradict those of the next. The single point also fixes the viewer's place in the scene, so that standing in the hall and looking at the wall feels like standing in the painted court.

questions.explanation: One vanishing point makes every receding line obey a single shared viewpoint, so the painted parts read as one coherent space rather than separate fragments. It also fixes where the viewer is expected to stand in relation to the scene.
questions.hint: Think about what a single point says about the viewer.

questions.hint: Multiply the nearest value by the stated fraction.

options.text: Mural three, because the horizon sits far above the floor of the scene and the figures are seen from above.
Mural one, because a point 1.6 metres up is about the height of a standing viewer.
options.misconception: confuses a low horizon with a high viewpoint

options.text: Mural two, because a vanishing point at the ceiling means the whole floor is seen from above.
options.misconception: reads a ceiling-level point as a raised viewpoint

options.text: All three, because any point above the floor gives a view from above.
options.misconception: makes every raised point a bird's-eye view

questions.explanation: A horizon four metres above the floor of the scene means the viewer is placed well above it, looking down on the figures, which is the bird's-eye construction. A point near standing eye level, one at the ceiling and the claim that any height works each describe something else.
questions.hint: Compare the height of the point with the figures.

That the passage was painted on fresh plaster and has lifted away from it.

options.misconception: invents a later repair to explain the loss

options.misconception: invents an oil medium to explain the flaking

stimulus.body: The site record for the library mural notes that it was painted on a stretched linen canvas in the studio over two winter months, then fixed to the wall with a wooden batten frame once the room was finished.

The picture was protected from the damp of the finished room by the batten frame.
options.misconception: credits the frame with damp protection

options.text: The picture was guaranteed to match the proportions of the wall by the stretching.
options.misconception: claims the stretching fixed the proportions

options.misconception: claims the mural was still reversible in situ

questions.explanation: Working on a canvas in the studio over two winter months meant the picture was finished comfortably before the room was finished, which is the point of the method. A damp-proof frame, proportions fixed by stretching and repainting in place are not what the record supports.
questions.hint: Read the record against the sequence of the work.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a thick body of paint changes the play of light on a wall.
questions.stem: Under the brief, the painter explains how the thickness of a passage affects the way it catches light. Give the explanation.

answer.exemplar: A thick body of paint stands away from the support and keeps the ridges of the brush, so each ridge holds a highlight on its crest and casts a small shadow on its lee side. The viewer therefore reads the surface as modelled by real relief rather than by drawn shadow, which is why heavy passages seem to shift as the viewer moves. A thin film lies flat and takes its modelling entirely from painted light and shade, so it behaves like a coloured drawing on the wall.

questions.explanation: A thick body of paint stands off the wall and keeps the ridges of the brush, so it catches real highlights and casts small real shadows that shift as the viewer moves. A thin film lies flat and can only model through painted light and shade.
questions.hint: Think about how the surface catches the light.

questions.learningObjective: Identify atmospheric depth by comparing values and sharpness across a landscape.
questions.stem: A survey compares two painted landscapes. In the first, the far hills are paler and cooler than the near fields and their outlines are soft. In the second, all the bands are equally bright and equally sharp. Which painting uses atmospheric depth?

options.text: The first, because it lowers contrast and cools the colour as the distance increases.
The second, because equal brightness keeps the picture calm and unified.
options.misconception: mistakes uniformity for depth

options.text: The second, because sharp outlines are needed to read the far hills at all.
options.misconception: claims sharpness is required for distance

options.text: Neither, because both fail to show the recession caused by perspective.
options.misconception: denies that tonal recession is depth

questions.learningObjective: State the requirement a fixed canvas mural places on its support.
questions.stem: For the concourse, the brief specifies a mural painted on canvas to be fixed to the wall. What must the fixer provide?

options.text: A rigid support that carries the canvas evenly, since a sagging cloth distorts the picture.
A humid cavity behind the canvas, so the fabric can breathe freely.
options.misconception: suggests a damp cavity helps the canvas

options.text: A flexible fixing, so that the canvas can move with the wall beneath it.
options.misconception: prescribes a flexible fixing that distorts the work

options.text: A perfectly smooth wall, since the canvas will take every bump in the masonry.
options.misconception: asks for a smooth wall behind the canvas

questions.stem: From the site record above, what do the colour differences between the sections indicate?

options.text: That the sections were laid at different times and have weathered to different degrees.
That the earlier section was painted with a different pigment from the later ones.
options.misconception: invents a pigment change to explain the tone

options.text: That the earlier section was cleaned, and the cleaning has left it paler.
options.misconception: invents a cleaning campaign for the difference

options.misconception: claims a complete repaint over the scheme

questions.explanation: Pale chalky tones in the earliest section and warmer saturation in later ones match lime that has carbonated and weathered for different lengths of time. A different pigment, cleaning and a complete repaint would not produce that ordered sequence.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a durable secco passage must be made on dry plaster.
questions.stem: The brief for the chapel porch requires a passage that must be executed on dry plaster. Explain what the painter must do to make that passage durable.

answer.exemplar: Because colour laid on dry plaster has no bond to the lime, the painter must first prepare the surface so that the paint has something to grip, then lay the colour in a body heavy enough to stay attached, and choose a medium that binds strongly within the paint itself. The same passage executed on fresh plaster would be carried by the lime as it carbonates, so on a dry wall every part of that adhesion has to be supplied by the layer and its preparation.

questions.explanation: With no bond from the lime, the painter must prepare the dry surface for grip, lay the colour in a body heavy enough to hold, and use a medium that binds firmly within the film. Everything the wet lime would have supplied must come from the paint itself.
questions.hint: Think about what the wet lime would normally provide.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Identify a one-point scheme from the behaviour of measured lines.
questions.stem: A survey of a painted stair hall measures the drawn lines of the treads, the string and the cornice. The treads recede and converge, while the cornice above runs parallel to the picture plane. Which scheme is in use?

options.text: A one-point scheme, with the receding lines converging and the cornice keeping its direction.
A two-point scheme, since the cornice also recedes towards the side of the picture.
options.misconception: treats a parallel cornice as a second vanishing set

options.text: An oblique scheme, since the treads are drawn at an angle across the picture.
options.misconception: mislabels orthogonal recession as oblique

options.text: No scheme at all, since the two sets of lines behave differently.
options.misconception: denies a scheme because the lines differ

questions.explanation: Converging treads with a cornice that keeps its direction is exactly the one-point arrangement, in which only the lines perpendicular to the picture plane converge. Two points, an oblique scheme and no scheme each misdescribe that geometry.
questions.hint: Ask which lines are perpendicular to the picture plane.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Plan the graded recession for a long painted distance.
questions.stem: First, the brief specifies that the painted city should recede for a distance of five kilometres. Second, the painter must plan the recession. Which plan best serves it?

options.text: Step the values and colours down in graded bands, with the furthest band palest and coolest.
Use one mid tone for all the buildings and let the perspective lines carry the recession.
options.misconception: relies on lines alone for the recession

options.text: Darken the far blocks so that they read as heavy masses behind the near ones.
options.misconception: darkens the distance instead of lightening it

options.text: Outline every block sharply so the eye can separate them at any distance.
options.misconception: sharpens outlines to separate the distance

questions.explanation: A long recession is built from graded bands in which value falls and colour cools with distance, and the painter must plan those steps in advance. A single mid tone, darkened far blocks and sharp outlines each work against the atmospheric recession.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a construction for a seated viewer differs from one for a standing viewer.
questions.stem: The brief for the reading room requires the painted corridor to be seen from a seated position. Explain how that affects the construction.

answer.exemplar: The horizon line stands at the height of the viewer's eye, so a construction intended to be read from a chair must place the vanishing point at seated eye level, well below the standing figure and far below the cornice. The whole scheme is then measured from that lowered point, which means the walls appear to rise above the viewer and the floor spreads gently rather than steeply. The picture therefore rewards a reader at a desk and tells a standing visitor that the room is meant for sitting.

questions.explanation: The horizon sits at eye level, so a scheme meant to be read from a chair must place its vanishing point at seated height, with the whole construction measured from that lowered point. The room then rises above the viewer rather than opening around them.
questions.hint: Think about the height of the eye that the picture assumes.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: State the mechanism by which distant forms are made to recede.
questions.stem: The brief for the painted valley specifies that the far ridge should read as more distant than the near hedge. Which statement best describes how that is achieved?

options.text: By lowering the contrast and cooling the colour of the far forms as the distance increases.
By enlarging the far ridge so that it fills more of the sky.
options.misconception: enlarges the distance instead of receding it

options.text: By giving the far ridge the strongest outline in the whole painting.
options.misconception: gives the far form the sharpest contour

options.text: By repeating the near hedge at the far end with a darker colour.
options.misconception: relies on repetition rather than tonal recession

questions.explanation: Atmospheric depth works by lowering contrast and cooling colour with distance, so the far ridge reads as further than the near hedge. Enlarging the far form, giving it the strongest outline and repeating the near forms all fail to produce that recession.
questions.hint: Think about how the air between changes what we see.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Locate a vanishing point relative to the horizon and the room.

stimulus.body: The architect's note records that the painted scene in the vestibule shows the horizon line at 2.4 metres above the vestibule floor, that the vestibule floor stands 1.1 metres above the hall floor, and that the vanishing point on that horizon is 3 metres to the right of the doorway.

questions.stem: According to the note above, which statement about the vanishing point is correct?

options.text: It lies on the horizon, above the hall floor and to the right of the doorway.
It lies at the eye level of a standing visitor in the vestibule.
options.misconception: assumes the point matches a standing eye level

options.text: It lies on the floor of the painted scene where the orthogonals begin.
options.misconception: puts the point at the base of the orthogonals

options.text: It lies on the horizon of the real hall rather than of the painted scene.
options.misconception: moves the point to the real room's horizon

questions.explanation: A vanishing point lies on the horizon line of its own construction, so a point 3 metres to the right of the doorway on a horizon 2.4 metres above the vestibule floor, itself 1.1 metres above the hall floor, lies on the horizon and above the hall floor. Standing eye level, the base of the orthogonals and the real hall's horizon are not established.
questions.hint: Ask what line the point must lie on.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why receding lines must reach a single vanishing point.
questions.stem: The brief for the painted vestibule asks why the orthogonals of the arcade must all reach the same vanishing point. Give the explanation.

answer.exemplar: Every orthogonal represents a line running directly away from the viewer, and all such lines in a single coherent view must appear to converge on the one point that corresponds to the direction of looking. If they were allowed to reach different points, the arcade would be drawn from several viewpoints at once, and the eye would read the result as a jumble rather than as a space. Sharing one point therefore guarantees that the painted architecture is seen from a single, identifiable place in the room.

questions.explanation: All lines running directly away from the viewer must appear to converge on the one point that matches the direction of looking, which is what makes the painted architecture read as a single space. Different points would mean several viewpoints at once and a jumbled result.
questions.hint: Think about where receding lines must meet.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Day-sized sections of a fresco wall
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the total time needed for a programme of daily sections.
questions.stem: The brief divides a wall of 96 square metres into day-sized sections of 8 square metres each, and allows 4 hours to lay and paint each section. How many hours are needed for the whole wall?
questions.explanation: The wall needs 96 divided by 8, which is 12 sections, and 12 sections at 4 hours each take 48 hours. Treating the whole wall as one section would give 4 hours and counting sections without multiplying by the time each takes leaves the hours unstated.
questions.hint: Find the number of sections, then multiply by the hours each.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A wall painting on a dry support
questions.learningObjective: Compare museum records to establish what can and cannot be moved.
questions.stem: The store of the museum records three accessions. One is a painting on canvas fixed to a wall in a hall that has since been redecorated. Another is a painting on plaster that cannot be removed. A third is a painting on canvas that was rolled and is now stored flat. What do these records show about the first and third?

options.text: That a canvas mural can be removed, transported and stored, while a painting on plaster cannot.
That all three were made on the same support but stored in different ways.
options.misconception: claims the support is the same in all three

options.text: That the canvas murals were made later than the plaster painting to replace it.
options.misconception: infers a chronological sequence from storage

options.text: That the rolling of the third mural caused the losses in the plaster painting.
options.misconception: links two unrelated records

questions.explanation: A canvas mural is an object that can be unhooked, rolled and stored, whereas a painting on plaster is bonded to the wall and cannot be moved, which the records show directly. A shared support, a chronological sequence and a causal link between the entries are not supported.
questions.hint: Compare what can be moved with what is fixed.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Decide how to match the depth of colour of a fresco in a secco passage.
questions.stem: First, the architect's brief specifies that a secco passage beside a fresco passage must match the fresco in depth of colour. Second, the painter must decide how to lay it. Which decision is sound?

options.text: Lay the secco passage with a heavier body of colour, since without the bond of wet lime it needs the thickness to hold.
Lay the secco passage as thinly as the fresco, so the two passages match at the surface.
options.misconception: matches surface without considering the bond

options.text: Grind the fresh pigment into the dry plaster before painting, so the passage behaves like a fresco.
options.misconception: impossible to grind pigment into a set surface

options.text: Apply the fresco passage over the secco passage so that the whole scheme shares one film.
options.misconception: proposes a reverse covering of the dry passage

questions.explanation: Matching the depth of colour on a dry wall requires a heavier body of paint, because without the bond of wet lime the film has only its own thickness to hold it. Laying it thin risks loss, grinding pigment into a set plaster does nothing, and covering the dry passage reverses the sequence.
questions.hint: Think about what the wet lime gives the fresco passage.
